title: Psalm 138: Thanks Before the Gods
summary: David gives thanks to the LORD with his whole heart, bowing toward the holy temple because God answered him on the day he called and gave him strength. He foresees all the kings of the earth praising the LORD when they hear his words, and he rests in the truth that the LORD, though high, regards the lowly. He closes confident that God will fulfill his purpose for him and asks him not to abandon the work of his hands.
story: Psalm 138 begins the last collection of psalms attributed to David in the Psalter, Psalms 138 to 145. The placement matters. It comes right after Psalm 137, where exiles in Babylon hung up their harps and asked how they could sing the LORD's song in a foreign land. Psalm 138 answers by singing, and by singing “before the gods”, in the presence of every rival power. Where Psalm 137 pictured foreign captors mocking Zion's songs, Psalm 138 pictures foreign kings giving thanks to the LORD. The final Davidic collection then moves through prayers for rescue (Psalms 140 to 143) to a royal psalm (144) and a great hymn to God's kingdom (145), leading into the closing Hallelujah psalms.
historical:
The heading reads simply “Of David.” The Hebrew phrase can mean written by David, belonging to a Davidic collection, or dedicated to David, and scholars disagree over how much weight to give such superscriptions. Traditional readers take them as reliable statements of authorship. Many modern scholars see them as later additions that record how the psalms were collected and read, though still ancient. The Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint, made by Jewish scholars in the last centuries BC) also attributes this psalm to David.

One detail has drawn attention to the date. Verse 2 speaks of bowing toward God's holy temple, and Solomon's temple was built only after David's death. Those who hold to Davidic authorship point out that the Hebrew word for temple (hekal, a palace or great house) was used earlier of the tabernacle at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9 and 3:3), so it could refer to the tent sanctuary of David's day. Others read the reference as evidence of a later date, in the time of the first or second temple. The psalm gives no clear occasion; it describes a rescue from trouble and enemies in general terms that fit many settings.
cultural:
Bowing down toward the temple reflects an ancient practice. Israelites away from the sanctuary faced toward it in prayer, as Solomon asked in his dedication prayer (1 Kings 8:29-30) and as Daniel did when he prayed toward Jerusalem from Babylon (Daniel 6:10). The temple was the place where God had set his name, the point on earth where heaven touched down.

The phrase “before the gods” in verse 1 has been read in several ways. It may refer to the gods of the nations, so that David praises the LORD in open defiance of rival deities. It may refer to the heavenly council, the spiritual beings who surround God's throne in texts such as Psalm 82:1. Some take it to mean human rulers or judges. The Septuagint translated it “before the angels.” Whichever sense is meant, the point is that the LORD's praise is sung in the presence of every other power that claims honor. The picture of the kings of the earth hearing God's words (verse 4) fits a world where kings were thought to rule by the favor of their own gods.
literary: Psalm 138 is an individual song of thanksgiving with a hymn-like middle. Verses 1 to 3 give thanks in the first person for a specific answer to prayer. Verses 4 to 6 widen the circle, picturing all the kings of the earth joining the praise and grounding it in a paradox: the LORD is on high, yet he attends to the lowly, while he knows the proud only from far away. Verses 7 and 8 return to the first person and look ahead with confidence into future trouble. The psalm ends in a prayer rather than a statement: “do not abandon the works of Your hands.” The movement from personal thanks to universal praise and back again shows that one person's rescue is meant to become a story the nations hear.

outline.t: The kings of the earth praise the LORD who regards the lowly
Confidence in trouble: the LORD will fulfill his purpose

doctrines.note: God is exalted and yet near to the lowly. His height does not make him distant from the weak; it is the proud, not the humble, whom he keeps at a distance. His loving devotion and faithfulness are the grounds of the psalmist's praise.
The psalm testifies that God answered on the day the psalmist called, and that the answer came as inner strength as well as outward rescue. Answered prayer leads to public thanksgiving.
The psalm pictures all the kings of the earth giving thanks to the LORD when they hear his words. Israel's praise is meant to reach the nations, anticipating the worship of every people.

words.note: Elohim, here the gods. The same Hebrew word can mean the one true God or gods in the plural, and context decides. In verse 1 it refers to powers other than the LORD, whether the gods of the nations, heavenly beings, or earthly rulers. The Septuagint read it as angels. The psalmist sings the LORD's praise in front of them all.

Shaphal, low or lowly. The word describes the humble and the humbled, people brought down by circumstance or who carry themselves without pride. Verse 6 sets them against the proud: God attends to the lowly and keeps the proud at a distance. It is one of the great reversals of Scripture, repeated in Hannah's song and in Mary's.

Gamar, to complete or bring to an end. In verse 8 the LORD will complete or fulfill what concerns the psalmist. The word expresses confidence that God finishes what he begins. The same verb appears in Psalm 57:2, where David calls on God who fulfills his purpose for him.

christ: The psalm's central paradox, that the LORD who is on high attends to the lowly, is the pattern of the gospel. Mary sings that God has looked on the humble state of his servant, brought down rulers, and lifted up the humble (Luke 1:48-52), and Paul describes Christ as the one who, though in the form of God, humbled himself and was then highly exalted (Philippians 2:6-11). The vision of all the kings of the earth giving thanks when they hear God's words anticipates the gospel going to the nations and the picture in Revelation of the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24). The psalm's closing confidence, that God will complete his purpose and not abandon the work of his hands, is echoed by Paul's conviction that he who began a good work will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6). These are thematic links rather than predictions, but they show the psalm's hope taken up in Christ.
questions: The psalmist sings his thanks before the gods, in the presence of rival powers. What rival claims on your loyalty make it hardest to give God wholehearted thanks?
Verse 6 says the LORD attends to the lowly but knows the proud from afar. What does it mean that pride puts distance between a person and God?
The psalm ends by asking God not to abandon the work of his hands. Where in your life do you need to trust that God will finish what he has begun?
